summary: Defines the Common Name Resolution Protocol, which lets people use everyday names, such as a company name or book title, to find resources instead of URLs. Because good URLs are often taken, a common name can be easier to remember and type.

plainLanguage.summary: It is easier to remember a shop's name than its long web address. CNRP is a way to type the name and have the computer find the right place.

questions: what is the common name resolution protocol
how can common names resolve to urls
what is a common name in cnrp
subtitle: A protocol for turning a plain word or phrase, like a company name or book title, into the resources it refers to.

tldr.problem: People remember names like a trade name or book title more easily than URLs, and good URLs for a resource are often already taken.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a small XML query containing a common name and optional hint properties to a resolution service, and gets back XML results made of resource descriptors, referrals and status messages, carried over HTTP on port 1096 or over SMTP.
tldr.outcome: It defines a minimal, extensible core for talking to common name resolution services. It is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 3367 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Common Names and Why They Need a Protocol
sections.content:
A common name is a word or a phrase, without imposed syntactic structure, that may be associated with a resource. The RFC's examples are "Internet Engineering Task Force" in an organization category and "Moby Dick" in a book category. Common names are not URIs: they lack URI syntax, and unlike URNs there is no requirement that the association between a name and a resource be unique or persistent.

The RFC describes two kinds of client: browser enhancements, where the address field accepts a common name instead of a URL, and search sites that offer name resolution as a complement to search. Either may talk to back-end resolution services.

The protocol is about resolution: retrieving data associated in advance with descriptors that match the request. Because descriptors need not be unique, zero or more records may come back. Resolution services are not generic search services, so no complex Boolean queries or relevance ranking are required. Service discovery, administration, name registration and ownership are outside the initial scope.
sections.plainLanguage: People remember names, not long addresses. CNRP lets you type a name and get back where it lives. It is like asking a librarian for a book by title and getting a shelf number.

sections.title: The Interaction Model
sections.content:
CNRP is a simple request and response protocol. A service offers name resolution at one or more servers. If a service keeps different collections on different servers, it SHOULD say which datasets each server offers, identifying each dataset by a URI. A server may also send a referral: a pointer to another service that can give further answers, passed on to the client instead of the server chaining the query itself.

All requests and responses are XML, using the DTD in Section 5, which is definitive if the descriptive examples disagree. There are two requests: a general query for a common name, and a service query asking for an object that describes the service and its capabilities. There is one type of response, a set of results containing result items, referrals and status messages.

The spec is independent of transport, but generic clients and servers MUST support HTTP on the default CNRP port, 1096. XML queries and responses MUST be UTF-8. All URIs MUST follow the absoluteURI production from RFC 2396.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand a note to a helper. The helper hands back a list of answers, and may say 'ask my friend down the road too'. Everything is written in one agreed note format, and the helper is reachable at a standard door number.

sections.title: Properties and Queries
sections.content:
Every CNRP object is a list of properties, each a named, typed attribute whose value is a string. The four core properties, which all services MUST support, are CommonName, ID (an opaque identifier for a result, not globally unique or necessarily persistent), resourceURI and description.

Services can add custom properties by defining a name and a type. Types are scoped to the property they are defined for, and custom properties MUST be registered with IANA. The optional base properties are language, geography, category, range and dataseturi. The default type for many properties is freeform, so a user can just type a value into a text field.

A query must hold one and only one common name or one and only one ID. Properties in a query are hints: a server accepts any correctly encoded property, but how far it honors them is a service differentiator, and results are the closest matches rather than an exact SQL-style filter. Different properties are implicitly ANDed, repeated values of the same property are ORed, and the order implies precedence. The special value, a single asterisk, stands for all admissible values. OR on the common name itself is not supported, and CNRP does not specify string equivalence rules for matching names.

Illustrative from the RFC: asking for BMW resources preferring German, then French, then any language, uses three language properties with values de-DE, fr-FR and an asterisk.
sections.plainLanguage: A question is a name plus optional wishes, like 'bmw, in German if you can'. The helper does its best to match your wishes but does not promise every answer fits.

sections.title: Results, Services, Datasets and Referrals
sections.content:
The results container can hold resource descriptors, status messages, referrals and schema. Results from one service are ordered by decreasing relevance; once results from several services are merged, they can no longer be ordered, though each service's own results stay in order.

A ResourceDescriptor describes an Internet resource and MUST include the resourceURI. It can also carry the common name, ID, description, language, geography and category, plus a reference to the service it came from. A Service object is identified by a serviceuri, and may list datasets and servers. A Dataset is a set of common-name-to-URI mappings, and using datasets is completely optional. A Server is identified by a serveruri in its transport's scheme. A service MUST have at least one server on the default CNRP port so a client can fetch the initial Service object.

A Referral is a placeholder for un-fetched results from another service and possibly dataset. It lets a client chain resolution across services. A proxy service can also aggregate results from several sub-services and tag each result with a service reference.

For loop detection, referrals can be handled in an application-specific way, as hints only, or with rigorous detection, where a visited node is a serviceuri plus dataseturi pair. Status 3.1.3 (datasets not supported), 3.1.4 (first dataset only) and 3.1.5 (this dataset not supported) tell the client which nodes to treat as visited.
sections.plainLanguage: An answer card names the thing and where it lives. A referral card says 'try this other helper'. The client keeps a list of helpers already asked so it does not go round in circles.

sections.title: Status Messages
sections.content:
A status object carries a code and a free-text description; only the code matters programmatically. Status messages cover CNRP operations only. Anything defined by the transport, such as HTTP security or SMTP mail failure, MUST be reported through the transport's own mechanism.

Codes follow the RFC 1893 style class.subject.detail. The class gives severity: 1 informational, 2 success, 3 partial success, 4 transient failure and 5 permanent failure. The subject is 0 for other or undefined, 1 for query related and 2 for service related. A recognized subject must be reported even if the detail is not recognized. Appendix B lists the predefined codes, for example 4.2.1 (the service was too busy) and 5.2.1 (this service is no longer available).
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with a number that says how things went, from 'just so you know' to 'this will never work, change your request'.

sections.title: Discovering a Service's Schema
sections.content:
A servicequery is a special request, sent as <cnrp> <servicequery/> </cnrp>, that asks a service to describe itself. Full discoverability is not required: returning a Service object with its serviceuri is a minimal yet sufficient compliant implementation.

Advanced services can return schema information: a property schema declaring the base and custom properties used (both existing and new ones MUST be declared), a service schema, a query schema for the query interface and a resource descriptor schema for results. Property references say whether a property is required or optional. In the RFC's example, a French cocktail recipe service accepts language in queries and returns both language and a custom cocktailrecipe property.
sections.plainLanguage: Before asking for anything, you can ask the helper, 'what kinds of questions can you answer?' and it hands back a menu.

sections.title: Transport: HTTP and SMTP
sections.content:
Two transports are specified. In either, the payload MUST use the application/cnrp+xml media type, with no charset attribute because CNRP is always UTF-8.

Over HTTP, the client sends a POST to the / path with Content-type and Accept set to application/cnrp+xml, and the body is the CNRP XML document. The reply comes back with the same content type. Over SMTP, the XML document is mailed to an endpoint, and the server mails the results to the originator. The RFC says SMTP is included to illustrate a protocol with a much different range of latency. A service MUST specify at least one SMTP target to be reachable this way. Any other transport MUST use a port other than the default CNRP port.
sections.plainLanguage: CNRP can be delivered like a web form submission or like an email. Either way the question and the answer are the same kind of note.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names three threats: man-in-the-middle attacks, malicious agents posing as a service by spoofing a Service object, and denial of service made easier by adding a level of indirection. For the first, it proposes transport-level authentication and encryption where available, or signing and encrypting entries or whole responses with the XML signature methods then being developed. For spoofing, the Service object should be signed. For denial of service, it offers no solution and only encourages providers to mitigate.

IANA registers well-known properties, property types and status messages, but not values or servers. Unregistered properties and types must start with x-. Registration is first come first served with no review, and IANA is also directed to register the application/cnrp+xml media type.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could pretend to be the helper or jam the line. Signing the helper's ID card and using locked delivery are the suggested protections.

items.label: Informational
items.desc: No bearing on the success or failure of a request.

items.label: Success
items.desc: The request was processed and results were returned.

items.label: Partial success
items.desc: Some values were invalid or ignored, but not as a true error.

items.label: Transient failure
items.desc: A temporary event prevented completion; retrying later may work.

items.label: Permanent failure
items.desc: Resending the same request is unlikely to help.
